general: The NYC Subway opened on October 27, 1904, with just 28 stations. Today there are 472 stations, the most of any subway system in the world.
Mayor George B. McClellan piloted the first subway train himself from City Hall to 103rd Street, refusing to give up the silver Tiffany & Co. handle.
Over 100,000 riders boarded on opening day in 1904, each paying just 5 cents for a ticket.
The subway system has 665 miles of revenue track and 850 total miles including non-revenue track - one of the world's longest.
The Great Blizzard of 1888 helped convince New Yorkers that underground transit was superior to elevated trains.
In the 1960s, you could enjoy champagne and a pretzel or bagel on a short-lived 'bar car' that ran between Times Square and South Ferry.
The first air-conditioned subway car was introduced in July 1967.
An armored money train transported all subway and bus fares to a secret room at 370 Jay Street in Brooklyn from 1951 to 2006.
During the pandemic recovery, ridership reached 1.195 billion in 2024, about 70% of pre-pandemic levels.
The subway operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week - one of the few transit systems in the world to do so.
IRT lines use numbers (1-7) because they were the first system. BMT and IND lines use letters because they merged into what's now called the B Division.
The city took over the privately operated IRT and BMT systems in 1940, creating a unified public transit network.
Alfred Ely Beach built NYC's first underground train in 1869-1870: a 312-foot pneumatic tube pushed by air pressure, with a station featuring a grand piano and chandeliers.
Beach built his pneumatic subway secretly at night under the cover story of a 'pneumatic mail system' to evade Boss Tweed's opposition.
When workers excavated the BMT Broadway Line in 1912, they discovered Beach's forgotten pneumatic tunnel, complete with the original subway car and piano.

Times Sq-42 St: The busiest subway station in the system with 54.3 million annual riders in 2023.
This massive complex joins four stations across multiple lines with a vast underground warren of connecting passageways.
When built in 1904, this area was called Longacre Square and wasn't the tourist destination it is today.
The station houses Roy Lichtenstein's 53-foot-long Times Square Mural, created in 1994.
You can still see remnants of the original 1904 station including a secret door to the Knickerbocker Hotel, original railings, and the first ticket booth.
The Times Square shuttle platforms are in what was originally the basement of the New York Times headquarters building.
A bombing here on October 12, 1960, injured 33 passengers.
In 2009, authorities foiled the Najibullah Zazi terror plot targeting this station and Grand Central.
Grand Central-42 St: The Chrysler Building has its own secret entrance to the 4/5/6 line. Walter Chrysler built it at his own expense after the IRT said no.
August Belmont Jr., president of the IRT and its main financier, had his own private subway car to travel from here to his racetrack at Belmont Park.
This station recorded the most OMNY contactless payments in 2023 with 5.4 million taps.
The Grand Central-Times Square shuttle is part of the original 1904 Contract I subway that ran continuously from City Hall.
City Hall: The abandoned City Hall station is the crown jewel of the original 1904 subway, designed by George Heins & Christopher LaFarge.
Closed on December 31, 1945, because its curving platform couldn't accommodate 10-car trains.
The station features stunning vaulted tile ceilings by master artisan Rafael Guastavino, chandeliers, and leaded skylights.
You can catch a glimpse by staying on the downtown 6 train at Brooklyn Bridge - it loops through City Hall to turn around.
Only New York Transit Museum members can take guided tours and actually step inside this beautiful ghost station.
WTC Cortlandt: This station was destroyed on September 11, 2001, and didn't reopen until September 8, 2018 - 17 years later.
It cost $181 million to rebuild the station with 1,200 feet of new track.
Artist Ann Hamilton created 'CHORUS,' a 4,350-square-foot white marble mosaic featuring text from the Declaration of Independence and the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The station has a direct entrance to the South Pool of the 9/11 Memorial, where the South Tower once stood.
No one in the subway system died during the 9/11 attacks because service was halted quickly after the first plane struck.
191 St: At 173 feet below street level, this is the deepest station in the entire subway system.
It's one of only a few stations that still has full-time elevator operators.
Access from street level requires taking four elevators, or walking through a 1,000-foot-long pedestrian tunnel to Broadway.
The station is near Manhattan's highest natural point in Washington Heights, creating the dramatic elevation change.
The graffiti-covered pedestrian tunnel is sometimes called NYC's only underground 'street.'
Smith-9 St: At 88 feet above street level, this is the highest subway station in the system - the opposite extreme from 191st Street.
Located in Brooklyn on the F and G lines, it offers dramatic views of the surrounding neighborhood.
125 St: Multiple 125th Street stations serve Harlem's 'Main Street,' which is co-named Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard.
The IND station features large-scale photographs of Harlem in the 1920s and 1930s.
The IRT Broadway-Seventh Avenue station sits on the Manhattan Valley Viaduct, a 2,174-foot landmark structure on the National Register of Historic Places.
The Apollo Theater is just one block away from the A/C/D station.
When the Lexington Avenue Line opened here in 1918, it triggered development throughout East Harlem.
In the early 20th century, this area was known as 'Harlem's 42nd Street' due to numerous vaudeville, burlesque, and film theaters.
Flushing-Main St: This station recorded the most MetroCard swipes in 2023 with 6.3 million.
The neighborhood is 60-75% Asian, mostly Chinese and Korean immigrants.
This is the eastern terminus of the 7 train, unofficially known as the 'International Express.'
Coney Island-Stillwell Av: This is the southernmost terminal in the entire subway system and one of the largest elevated terminals in the world.
The station opened in 1919-1920 when Coney Island was the primary summer resort for the entire New York metro area.
Rail service to Coney Island dates back to 1864 with the Brooklyn, Bath and Coney Island Railroad.
The station was completely renovated from 2001-2004 with a terracotta facade imitating the historic terminal.
You're steps away from the Wonder Wheel, the Cyclone roller coaster, and the original Nathan's Famous hot dog stand.
Nathan Handwerker started selling hot dogs here in 1916 for just a nickel each.
Bedford Av: This is the busiest subway station in Brooklyn outside of Downtown Brooklyn, with 9.4 million annual riders in 2015.
In the 1970s, only 1.2 million people used this station annually. Gentrification caused ridership to explode.
Bedford Avenue is the first subway stop in Brooklyn when traveling from Manhattan on the L train.
The station sits at the heart of hipster culture in Williamsburg, though the neighborhood has transformed dramatically since the 2005 re-zoning.
Until 2008, Williamsburg was a working-class mix of Poles, Italians, Hasidic Jews, and a small artist community.
Court St: This decommissioned station is now home to the New York Transit Museum.
The station was used for filming 'The Taking of Pelham One Two Three' in 1974. The MTA charged $250,000 plus $75,000 for insurance.

1: The 1 train serves 191st Street, the deepest station in the system at 173 feet below street level.
This line is part of the original IRT system that opened in 1904.
2: The 2 is part of the IRT West Side Line, one of the original 1904 routes.
3: The 3 serves Harlem along Lenox Avenue, connecting to historic neighborhoods and the Apollo Theater area.
4: The 4 train has a secret entrance from the Chrysler Building at Grand Central.
This is one of the original IRT lines from 1904.
5: The 5 train serves the historic 125th Street corridor in Harlem.
6: The 6 train was the line hijacked in the classic 1974 film 'The Taking of Pelham One Two Three.'
If you stay on the downtown 6 at Brooklyn Bridge, it loops through the abandoned City Hall station - the most beautiful station in the system.
The 6 still uses the City Hall station loop as a turnaround, though trains haven't stopped there since 1945.
Jennifer Lopez used to ride the 6 train to her dance studio. Her debut album 'On the 6' is named after this line.
7: The 7 is nicknamed the 'International Express' because it travels through neighborhoods where over 100 languages are spoken.
This was the principal subway route to the 1964-65 World's Fair in Queens.
Duke Ellington's signature tune 'Take the A Train' isn't about this line, but the 7 has inspired documentaries about immigrant journeys.
The express 7 train between 74th Street and Mets-Willets Point is the fastest end-to-end service, taking just 27 minutes.
Along the route, demographics shift dramatically: 60-75% Asian in Flushing, 40-60% Latino in Jackson Heights and Woodside.
A 2000 documentary called 'The #7 Train: An Immigrant Journey' celebrates the diversity along this line.
A: The A train is the longest subway line in the system at 31 miles, stretching from Inwood in northern Manhattan to Far Rockaway in southeast Queens.
For just $2.75, you can ride for over two hours through three boroughs and 36 stops (65 at night).
Duke Ellington made this line famous with his signature tune 'Take the A Train,' written by Billy Strayhorn.
The A line opened in 1932 as part of the first city-operated IND system.
Ella Fitzgerald often opened her shows with 'Take the A Train.'
B: The B is part of the former BMT/IND systems, now called the B Division.
The oldest structure still in use on the B Division opened in 1885.
C: The C serves historic 125th Street in Harlem with a station featuring 1920s-30s photographs.
The C line operates on tracks that were part of the first city-owned IND system from 1932.
D: The D train terminates at Coney Island, the southernmost station and one of the world's largest elevated terminals.
This line serves the iconic Coney Island boardwalk, Nathan's Famous, and historic amusement parks.
E: The E serves the World Trade Center Cortlandt station, which was rebuilt after being destroyed on 9/11.
F: The F train uses the 63rd Street Tunnel, which was built using a unique method: precast in the South, floated to NYC, then dropped into trenches in the East River.
The F terminates at Coney Island, steps from the Wonder Wheel and Cyclone roller coaster.
G: The G is the only line that doesn't enter Manhattan, running entirely through Brooklyn and Queens.
J: The J line includes the oldest structure still in use - portions dating to 1885 on the BMT Jamaica Line.
L: The L train saw dramatic ridership increases in the early 2000s due to gentrification in Williamsburg and other Brooklyn neighborhoods.
Bedford Avenue, the first Brooklyn stop, is the busiest station in Brooklyn outside Downtown.
The L line opened in 1924 as part of the BMT Canarsie Line.
M: The M serves neighborhoods in Brooklyn, Queens, and Manhattan.
N: The N train is part of the historic BMT system, serving both Manhattan and Brooklyn.
The N terminates at Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue.
Q: The Q serves some of the busiest stations in the system including Times Square.
The Q also terminates at Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue.
R: The R serves Times Square, the busiest station complex in the system.
You can walk the entire length of Alfred Ely Beach's 1870 pneumatic tube from the R/W City Hall station.
S: The Times Square-Grand Central Shuttle is part of the original 1904 Contract I subway.
When the north-south lines were extended in 1915-1918, the original crosstown connection was severed and became this shuttle.
From the shuttle platform at Times Square, you can see exposed infrastructure from the original 1904 tracks.
W: The W shares tracks with the R line through lower Manhattan.

history: The IRT (Interborough Rapid Transit) was the first subway system, opening October 27, 1904. It now operates as the A Division with numbered lines.
The BMT (Brooklyn-Manhattan Transit) evolved from the BRT after bankruptcy in 1923. It signed Dual Contracts with the city in 1913 to expand service.
The IND (Independent) opened in 1932 as the first city-owned and operated subway system.
The city unified all three systems in 1940, taking over the BMT on June 1 and the IRT on June 12.
The NYCTA (NYC Transit Authority) was created in 1953, followed by the state-level MTA in 1968.
The oldest subway structure still in use opened in 1885 on what's now the BMT Jamaica Line in Brooklyn.
Subway fares started at 5 cents in 1904. When the fare went to 15 cents in 1953, tokens were invented because no 15-cent coin existed.
Tokens were made of ferrous metal to be slightly magnetic - they were never successfully counterfeited.
MetroCards launched on January 6, 1994, at just two Lower Manhattan stations. Token use ended May 3, 2003.
OMNY contactless payment launched May 31, 2019. MetroCard sales end December 31, 2025, though they'll work through 2026.
Currently 65% of riders use OMNY instead of MetroCards.
The Joralemon Street Tube was NYC's first underwater subway tunnel, opening January 9, 1908, connecting Bowling Green to Brooklyn Borough Hall.
Construction on underwater tunnels involved workers digging by hand through riverbed mud, placing cast-iron rings and shields to block water.
Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 flooded 9 of the system's 14 underwater tunnels.
In 1885, the first elevated rail structure was built. The 1904 subway eventually replaced most elevated lines in Manhattan.
engineering: Nine underwater tunnels cross the East River, connecting Manhattan to Brooklyn and Queens.
Subway tunnels aren't exactly underwater - they're built about 30 feet below the riverbed, protected by 50 feet of water above.
The deepest point of the Joralemon Street tubes is 91-95 feet below the mean high water level of the East River.
Original construction used 'cut-and-cover' method: tear up the street, dig the tunnel, then cover it back up.
Modern construction uses Tunnel Boring Machines (TBMs) like 'Adi,' which dug the Second Avenue Subway tunnels.
The 63rd Street Tunnel was precast in the South, floated to New York, and dropped into trenches dug in the East River.
Clifford Milburn Holland designed four subway tunnels across the East River including the Clark Street, 14th Street, 60th Street, and Montague Street tunnels.
According to former MTA official Michael Horodniceanu: 'There is no such thing as a tunnel that doesn't have leaks.'
The Manhattan Valley Viaduct at 125th Street is a 2,174-foot elevated structure that's a designated NYC landmark.
The system includes 248 miles of routes but 850 total miles of track when you count non-revenue trackage.
IRT infrastructure is too small for B Division (BMT/IND) cars, so the systems remain physically separate despite operational unification.
movies: The first motion picture ever shot in the subway system was 'City Hall to Harlem in 15 Seconds via the Subway Route' in 1904 by Edwin S. Porter for Thomas Edison.
The 1974 film 'The Taking of Pelham One Two Three' is so influential that the MTA still avoids 1:23 as a departure time for Pelham trains.
'Pelham' inspired 'Die Hard' and its color-coded criminals inspired 'Reservoir Dogs.' It was remade in 1998 and 2009.
'The Warriors' (1979) shows heavily graffitied cars from the Bronx to Coney Island - a stark contrast to today's clean trains.
'The French Connection' (1971) features a famous chase scene filmed without city permission under the elevated line in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn.
'On the Town' starring Frank Sinatra and Gene Kelly was one of the first movies to feature the NYC subway in Technicolor.
Marilyn Monroe's iconic dress-blowing scene was filmed over a subway grate at 52nd and Lexington on September 15, 1954.
Michael Jackson's 'Bad' music video was filmed at the Hoyt-Schermerhorn station platform.
Sylvester Stallone played an unnamed subway mugger in an early Woody Allen comedy, five years before 'Rocky.'
'The Brave One' (2007) used the unused express tracks at Church Avenue for filming.
The Court Street station (now the Transit Museum) has been used for many films since it closed in 1946.
celebrities: Jennifer Lopez regularly rode the 6 train to her dance studio. Her debut album 'On the 6' is named after this line.
Robin Williams busked as a mime outside the Museum of Modern Art while studying at Juilliard.
Alice Tan Ridley, a gospel singer who performs in the subway, was featured on America's Got Talent Season 5.
Guitarist Kaki King practiced in the subway before making it big and performing at Carnegie Hall.
August Belmont Jr., president and financier of the IRT, had his own private subway car to travel to Belmont Park racetrack.
music: Duke Ellington's signature tune 'Take the A Train' by Billy Strayhorn became one of the most famous jazz standards.
Music Under New York (MUNY) was established in 1987 after musician Roger Manning successfully challenged the performance ban in court in 1985.
Over 350 artists and groups participate in MUNY, performing at about 30 high-traffic stations.
Performers must pass rigorous annual auditions to join MUNY, though any musician can legally perform in the system.
You can perform on platforms but not in subway cars, within 25 feet of a booth, or using amplification devices.
'Showtime' performances are technically illegal on trains but commonly seen on express trains.
The 'Saw Lady' Natalia Paruz is famous for playing the musical saw in subway stations.
Flexing, a type of street dance that originated in Brooklyn, is commonly performed throughout the system.
Times Square and Union Square stations have common areas where multiple lines converge - popular spots for performers.
neighborhoods: Harlem transformed during the Great Migration of the 1910s-20s when the subway opened up the neighborhood to African Americans from the South.
The Apollo Theater area was known as 'Harlem's 42nd Street' in the vaudeville era of the early 20th century.
Williamsburg was a working-class Polish, Italian, and Hasidic neighborhood until artists moved in during the 1970s, fleeing Manhattan's high rents.
By 2008, Williamsburg had become an icon of hipster culture, making it cost-prohibitive for the artists who originally redefined it.
Flushing's Main Street area is 60-75% Asian, mostly Chinese and Korean immigrants who arrived after immigration law changes.
Jackson Heights, Woodside, and Elmhurst along the 7 train are 40-60% Latino with residents speaking over 100 languages combined.
Coney Island was New York's primary summer resort when the Stillwell Avenue terminal opened in 1919-1920.
The opening of the 125th Street station on the Lexington Line in 1918 triggered development throughout East Harlem.
The 7 train corridor is documented in the 2000 film 'The #7 Train: An Immigrant Journey' about ethnic diversity.
trivia: The silver Tiffany & Co. handle from the first subway ride in 1904 is displayed at the New-York Historical Society.
Boss Tweed opposed the subway because it would hurt profits from elevated railroads, so Alfred Beach built his pneumatic tube in secret.
Beach's pneumatic subway charged 25 cents per ride (about $6 in 2024) but still attracted 400,000 riders in its first year.
The ban on subway performance was ruled unconstitutional in 1985, leading to the creation of Music Under New York.
Tokens went through five different versions from 1953 to 2003 and were made magnetic to prevent counterfeiting.
MetroCards have a chamfer (diagonal cutout) at the top right corner and a circular hole on the left to ensure proper reading.
OMNY readers can display 11 different screens depending on payment success and reader functionality.
The 191st Street pedestrian tunnel is sometimes called NYC's only underground 'street' and is famous for graffiti.
Smith-9th Street in Brooklyn is the highest station at 88 feet above street level - offering dramatic views.
The Wonder Wheel, Cyclone roller coaster, and Nathan's Famous have all been at Coney Island for close to 100 years.
During construction of the original subway, workers used cut-and-cover method, which meant tearing up entire streets.
The Great Blizzard of 1888 paralyzed the city and convinced planners that underground transit was essential.
There are 472 stations in the NYC Subway - more than any other transit system in the world.
The system operates 24/7, making it one of only a handful of transit systems worldwide with round-the-clock service.
You can ride 31 miles on the A train for just $2.75 - from Inwood to Far Rockaway, taking over 2 hours.
